## Original idea
{
  "title": "Beyond Step-Local Verification: Tracing Perception Error Cascades in Multimodal Process Reward Models",
  "core_problem": "Multimodal process reward models verify each reasoning step independently, missing cascade errors: steps where local reasoning is valid but produces wrong results because upstream visual information was misperceived. When a VLM misreads '45 degrees' as '90 degrees' in step 2, steps 3-7 may apply flawless trigonometry to the wrong angle -- appearing locally correct but systematically producing wrong answers. Cascade errors are invisible to binary correct/incorrect labels, to simple perception/reasoning classification (the cascade step's own reasoning IS correct), and even to Perceval's hallucination detection (no hallucination occurs at the cascade step itself). Across 4+ independent studies, 67-87% of VLM errors originate from visual perception, and each perception error can corrupt multiple downstream steps. Yet no existing verification method detects cascade errors: EVPV explicitly flags step-local cascade tracking as future work; MMErroR explicitly excludes cascading errors from evaluation; PARC models accumulation errors but only in text-only settings. Cascade-aware verification requires a fundamentally new capability: dependency-aware step evaluation that traces visual information flow through reasoning chains.",
  "opportunity": "Three converging developments make cascade-aware multimodal PRMs both timely and feasible. (1) The cascade detection gap is now explicitly acknowledged. EVPV/Grounding the Score (March 2026) uses global reliability signals for visual premise verification but states that 'step-local reliability is an important next step' -- precisely our contribution. MMErroR (Jan 2026) explicitly excludes cascading errors from their benchmark, acknowledging the gap without filling it. Hallucination propagation research (arXiv 2603.27201) empirically shows that cascade errors produce 'locally plausible, internally coherent' steps that mask underlying errors, motivating detection. (2) Text-only cascade detection proves the concept. PARC (Feb 2025) models 'accumulation errors' via premise-augmented DAGs in text-only reasoning, distinguishing root-cause from propagated errors. Conditional Reward Modeling (CRM, 2025) captures causal relationships among reasoning steps. ReasonDiag (March 2026) finds ~44.5% of verification false positives stem from error propagation. These demonstrate that dependency-aware verification is valuable -- extending it to the multimodal perception-reasoning boundary is the natural next step. (3) Dimensional and typed PRM approaches have matured but plateaued at step-independent evaluation. GM-PRM evaluates {visual alignment, reasoning logic} independently per step but cannot trace cross-step dependencies. PathFinder-PRM shows typed labels help in text-only (+2.2 PRMBench) but their ablation reveals that hierarchical structure matters more than category labels alone (-2.8 vs -0.4 on PRMBench). Perceval detects hallucinated spans but treats each step independently. The missing capability across all approaches is dependency-aware verification -- and the multimodal setting, where perception errors cascade from visual processing into reasoning chains, creates the strongest need for it.",
  "landscape": "The landscape segments into five clusters, none occupying CascadePRM's position at the intersection of multimodal perception-awareness and dependency-aware verification.

**Cluster A -- Step-Independent Multimodal PRMs.** Training VL-PRMs (arXiv 2509.23250) provides VL-PRM300K (1.32M steps) with binary labels despite noting 86% perception errors. VisualPRM (arXiv 2503.10291) provides VisualProcessBench (26,950 human labels), binary only. DreamPRM-1.5, TIM-PRM, VRPRM, MM-PRM, URSA all produce binary step scores. All evaluate each step independently without modeling cross-step information flow.

**Cluster B -- Perception-Aware Step-Independent Verification.** Perceval (arXiv 2604.24583, April 2026) detects hallucinated spans via token-level binary classification -- closest existing work, but treats each step independently and cannot distinguish cascade errors from direct errors. GM-PRM (arXiv 2508.04088) evaluates {step intent, visual alignment, reasoning logic} as structured CoT for generative scoring, but evaluations are step-independent with no cross-step dependency modeling; dimensions serve as training scaffolding producing a single Final Judgment score, not structured error labels; and no ablation demonstrates the value of separate dimensions. EVPV/Grounding the Score (arXiv 2603.16253) computes visual reliability via checklist verification, but uses candidate-level (global) rather than step-local reliability, and explicitly identifies step-local cascade tracking as future work.

**Cluster C -- Perception-Aware RL Optimization (Downstream).** PAPO (ICLR 2026, arXiv 2507.06448) uses implicit perception loss via masked-image KL divergence in GRPO -- no PRM involvement. VPPO (ICLR 2026, arXiv 2510.09285) reweights by visual dependency tokens. AT-RL (arXiv 2602.11455), PRCO (arXiv 2603.28618), Perception-R1 (ICLR 2026), PDCR (May 2026), and 'Bad Seeing or Bad Thinking' (ICML 2026 Spotlight) all operate at RL reward/policy level. These consume PRM outputs as scalar rewards; cascade-aware PRM outputs would directly improve the quality of signals these methods consume.

**Cluster D -- Text-Only Dependency-Aware Verification.** PARC (arXiv 2502.02362) introduces 'accumulation errors' via premise-augmented DAGs, distinguishing root-cause from propagated errors -- the closest text-only analog to cascade detection, but no multimodal component. CRM (arXiv 2509.26578) captures causal relationships among text reasoning steps via conditional probability chains. ReasonDiag (arXiv 2603.21286) visualizes error propagation patterns in text-only CoT, finding ~44.5% of verification false positives from error propagation. RewardFlow (arXiv 2603.18859) uses topology-aware propagation in state graphs. All are text-only and do not address the perception-reasoning boundary.

**Cluster E -- Error Taxonomies Without Cascade Detection.** PathFinder-PRM (arXiv 2505.19706) uses {math, consistency} types in text-only PRMs with modest gains (+2.2 PRMBench, but ablation shows category separation contributes only -0.4 vs -2.8 for hierarchical structure). ErrorRadar (ICLR 2025 Workshop) provides {visual perception, calculation, reasoning, knowledge, misinterpretation} for benchmarking MLLM error detection -- never for PRM training. MMErroR (arXiv 2601.03331) defines {visual perception, knowledge, comprehension, reasoning} but explicitly states: 'each sample contains a single, coherent reasoning error... real-world reasoning failures often involve cascading or multiple simultaneous errors.' ThinkWithImages-PRMBench (arXiv 2602.08346) defines 7 error types across 4 categories -- none is a cascade error. All taxonomies evaluate errors at the individual step level without modeling cross-step propagation.

**CascadePRM's unique position**: We bridge Cluster B (multimodal perception-aware verification) with Cluster D (dependency-aware verification) to detect cascade errors -- the gap explicitly acknowledged by EVPV, excluded by MMErroR, and unaddressed by any existing multimodal PRM.",
  "inspired_by": "Three conceptual bridges define CascadePRM's contribution. (1) PARC's accumulation error framework proves that distinguishing root-cause from propagated errors improves text-only verification, but the perception-reasoning boundary in multimodal settings creates a far more impactful instance of this problem: upstream perception failures cascade through downstream reasoning in ways that are mechanistically distinct from text-only logical propagation, because the root cause is cross-modal (visual processing failure) while the cascade is within-modal (text reasoning). (2) EVPV's explicit limitation creates our opportunity: their global reliability signal attenuates all steps uniformly when visual reliability is low, but cascade errors require step-local analysis -- a step that doesn't reference the image at all can still be a cascade error if it uses a value derived from an earlier misperception. The EVPV authors themselves identify step-local reliability as the 'important next step.' (3) PathFinder-PRM's ablation reveals that hierarchical structure (error detection guiding reward prediction) matters more than error type labels alone (-2.8 vs -0.4 on PRMBench). This insight shapes our approach: rather than simply classifying error types, we build a dependency-aware hierarchy where cascade detection (which requires reasoning about cross-step information flow) provides richer structural information than flat type classification. The counterfactual formalization -- 'would this step be correct if the upstream perception were corrected?' -- provides an objective, testable definition of cascade errors that avoids the subjectivity concerns of purely categorical error typing.",
  "approach": "We propose CascadePRM, a framework for detecting and leveraging perception error cascades in multimodal reasoning verification, comprising four interlocking components: (1) a counterfactual cascade detection algorithm, (2) a cascade-annotated benchmark and dataset, (3) cascade-aware PRM training, and (4) downstream integration demonstrating infrastructure value.

**Component 1: Counterfactual Cascade Detection Algorithm (Primary Novelty, Weeks 1-7).**

We formalize cascade errors and build an automated detection pipeline in four stages:

(Stage 1) Visual Claim Extraction: For each step in a solution, extract all claims that reference information derived from the image (e.g., 'angle ABC = 45 deg', 'the bar for 2020 shows 3.2M'). Uses a VLM (Qwen2.5-VL-72B) with targeted prompts to identify visual claims vs. pure reasoning statements.

(Stage 2) Information Flow Graph Construction: Build a directed acyclic graph (DAG) where nodes are reasoning steps and edges connect step j to step k if step k uses a quantity, relationship, or fact derived from visual claims in step j (directly or transitively). This extends PARC's premise-augmented DAG framework from text-only logical dependencies to cross-modal visual-to-reasoning dependencies.

(Stage 3) Perception Error Identification: For each step containing visual claims, verify claims against the image using ensemble VLM voting (Qwen2.5-VL-72B, InternVL2.5-78B, Gemini-2.5-Flash). Steps with incorrect visual claims verified by majority vote are labeled as root-cause perception errors. Dedicated perception verification extracts the specific claim and independently checks it with a focused prompt.

(Stage 4) Counterfactual Cascade Verification: For each downstream step k depending (via the DAG) on a root-cause perception error at step j: (a) extract the misperceived value from step j and determine the correct value; (b) construct a counterfactual prompt: 'Given that [quantity] is actually [correct_value] rather than [misperceived_value], is the reasoning in step k valid?'; (c) if the reasoning IS locally valid (confirmed by 2/3 VLMs), label step k as a CASCADE error; (d) if the reasoning is NOT locally valid, label as a direct error (reasoning, calculation, etc.). This counterfactual test provides an objective, testable definition unprecedented in the multimodal PRM literature.

**Component 2: Cascade-Annotated Benchmark and Dataset (Weeks 2-8).**

(Phase A) Gold-Standard Benchmark -- VisualProcessBench-Cascade: Extend VisualProcessBench's 2,866 samples (~8,000 incorrect steps) with cascade annotations. For each incorrect step, annotators (6 graduate-level, STEM backgrounds) assign: (i) a 3-tier error type {perception, reasoning, cascade} as the core taxonomy; (ii) an optional fine-grained subtype for non-cascade errors {perception subtypes: spatial/numerical/object/attribute; reasoning subtypes: symbolic_formulation/calculation/logical_deduction}; (iii) for cascade errors: the root-cause step ID and the misperceived value. Target inter-annotator agreement: Cohen's kappa > 0.65 for 3-tier classification (substantially above chance for 3-way), with agreement reported at all granularity levels: binary, 2-way {root-cause vs. cascade}, 3-tier, and full fine-grained. The cascade category is operationalized via the counterfactual question ('would this step be correct with corrected perception?'), which is more objective than purely categorical error typing.

(Phase B) Large-Scale Dataset -- VL-PRM-Cascade: Apply the automated cascade detection pipeline (Component 1) to VL-PRM300K (1.32M steps). Confidence-calibrated labeling: HIGH confidence (3/3 VLM agreement, ~70-75%) used directly; MEDIUM (2/3, ~15-20%) used with reduced weight; LOW (~10-15%) routed to human review. Validate against gold benchmark, targeting >80% cascade detection F1.

Pre-committed granularity fallback: If 3-tier kappa falls below 0.60, we report the {root-cause error vs. cascade error} binary taxonomy, which should achieve kappa > 0.70 as a binary classification with an objective counterfactual criterion. This turns a potential weakness into a controlled granularity ablation.

**Component 3: Cascade-Aware PRM Training (Weeks 7-12).**

Train multimodal PRMs (InternVL2.5-8B backbone) with five training regimes forming a granularity ladder:

(A) Binary baseline: standard correct/incorrect on VL-PRM300K.
(B) 2-way typed: {perception error, reasoning error} -- the simplest typed approach, similar in spirit to GM-PRM's dimensional separation but as explicit training labels.
(C) 3-way cascade-aware (PRIMARY MODEL): {perception, reasoning, cascade} with a two-stage prediction architecture inspired by PathFinder-PRM's hierarchical insight: first predict error type (perception/reasoning/cascade), then predict correctness conditioned on error type. For cascade errors, the model additionally predicts the root-cause step, providing interpretable error provenance.
(D) 3-way with cascade-weighted loss: same taxonomy as (C) but with cascade-specific loss weighting. Cascade errors receive higher weight because they represent the largest information gain over binary labels (a cascade step is wrong but for external reasons, requiring different correction strategies). Loss: L = sum_i w(type_i) * CE(y_i, y_hat_i) where w(cascade) > w(perception) > w(reasoning).
(E) Full fine-grained (ablation): complete sub-category decomposition for maximal information, reported for completeness.

Compare against: binary VL-PRM-7B, Perceval (binary hallucination PRM), GM-PRM (dimensional CoT), and EVPV (global reliability gating).

**Component 4: Downstream Integration -- EVPV Enhancement (Weeks 10-13).**

Demonstrate that cascade-aware PRM labels improve downstream verification by enhancing EVPV's framework:

(Integration A) Replace EVPV's global reliability signal with CascadePRM's step-local cascade scores. Instead of attenuating all steps uniformly when visual reliability is low, attenuate only steps identified as cascade-dependent (via the information flow DAG). Steps with no visual dependency path are scored at full weight regardless of global reliability.

(Integration B) Cascade-aware advantage weighting for RL: following DRM's multi-dimensional GRPO framework (arXiv 2510.11457), provide separate advantage signals for perception-error steps (which need better visual grounding) and cascade steps (which need upstream correction, not local improvement). This validates that typed PRM signals can improve RL training -- a mechanism proven feasible by Fine-Grained RLHF (NeurIPS 2023) and POW3R (arXiv 2605.20164) but never demonstrated with multimodal error types.

**Phase 5: Evaluation and Ablations (Weeks 10-15).**

Evaluate on: (a) VisualProcessBench-Cascade: step-level F1 for binary correctness, 3-way error type classification, and cascade detection accuracy (precision/recall/F1 specifically for identifying cascade steps); (b) downstream Best-of-N reranking on MathVista, MathVision, WeMath, ChartQA, PuzzleVQA with N=8,16,64; (c) EVPV integration: step-local vs. global reliability on the same benchmarks; (d) cascade-specific analysis: performance stratified by cascade depth (how many steps from the root perception error), visual modality (geometry/charts/tables), and cascade frequency.

Key ablations forming the granularity ladder: (i) {binary} -> {perception vs. reasoning} -> {perception, reasoning, cascade} -> {full fine-grained} to isolate cascade detection's marginal contribution; (ii) with/without counterfactual verification in cascade detection (does the counterfactual step improve over simple dependency-based cascade labeling?); (iii) cascade-weighted vs. uniform loss; (iv) head-to-head vs. GM-PRM's dimensional CoT approach on cascade-heavy problems; (v) annotation quality: high-confidence-only vs. all labels vs. human-verified.

**Expected Results and Contingency.** Primary hypothesis: the 3-way cascade-aware model (C) will outperform binary PRMs by +3-5 on VisualProcessBench step-level F1 and +2-3 on Best-of-N, with disproportionately large gains on geometry and diagram problems where cascade errors are most frequent. The granularity ladder will show that the {perception, reasoning} -> {perception, reasoning, cascade} step provides the largest marginal improvement, validating cascade detection as the primary value driver. EVPV integration will show +1-2 on benchmarks where EVPV already works. Conservative scenario: if overall gains are modest, the cascade error characterization (frequency, depth distribution, modality stratification) and released artifacts (VisualProcessBench-Cascade, VL-PRM-Cascade, cascade detection pipeline) are publishable contributions as the first empirical study of cascade error propagation in multimodal reasoning verification.",

  "description": "Current multimodal process reward models evaluate each reasoning step independently, missing cascade errors -- steps where local reasoning is valid but produces wrong results because upstream visual information was misperceived. A VLM that misreads a diagram angle cascades the error through all subsequent trigonometric calculations, producing steps that appear locally correct but are systematically wrong. This phenomenon is invisible to binary labels, simple perception/reasoning classification, and even perception-centric PRMs like Perceval (which detect hallucinations at the error source but not at cascade steps where no hallucination occurs). We propose CascadePRM, a framework for detecting and leveraging perception error cascades in multimodal reasoning verification. The core contribution is a counterfactual cascade detection algorithm: we build information flow DAGs tracing how visual claims propagate through reasoning chains, identify root-cause perception errors via ensemble VLM verification, then verify each downstream dependent step with a counterfactual test -- 'would this step be correct if the upstream perception were corrected?' This extends PARC's text-only accumulation error framework to the multimodal perception-reasoning boundary and fills the gap explicitly identified by EVPV (step-local reliability as future work) and excluded by MMErroR (cascading errors). We create VisualProcessBench-Cascade by annotating ~8,000 incorrect steps with cascade labels and root-cause provenance, generate cascade annotations for VL-PRM300K (1.32M steps) via the automated pipeline, and train cascade-aware PRMs with a two-stage hierarchical architecture (error type prediction guiding correctness scoring). A granularity ladder ablation -- {binary} to {perception, reasoning} to {perception, reasoning, cascade} to {full fine-grained} -- isolates cascade detection's marginal contribution, which we hypothesize is the largest single step. We demonstrate downstream value via EVPV integration, replacing global reliability with step-local cascade-aware scores, and via cascade-aware RL advantage weighting following DRM's multi-dimensional GRPO framework. We predict +3-5 on VisualProcessBench step-level F1 and +2-3 on Best-of-N across MathVista, MathVision, WeMath, ChartQA, and PuzzleVQA, with disproportionate gains on geometry and diagram problems where cascades are most frequent. Released artifacts: VisualProcessBench-Cascade (first cascade-annotated multimodal verification benchmark), VL-PRM-Cascade (cascade-annotated training dataset), and the counterfactual cascade detection pipeline.",

No existing error taxonomy includes cascade errors as a labeled category (not ErrorRadar's 5 types, not MMErroR's 4 types, not ThinkWithImages-PRMBench's 7 types, not PathFinder-PRM's 2 types). No existing PRM can distinguish cascade errors from direct errors. The counterfactual test ('would this step be correct if the upstream perception were corrected?') is unprecedented in multimodal PRM literature. PARC provides text-only accumulation error detection but does not address the cross-modal perception-reasoning boundary. The error taxonomy becomes infrastructure for cascade detection rather than the headline contribution. PathFinder-PRM's own ablation validates our reframing: their category separation contributes only -0.4 on PRMBench vs -2.8 for hierarchical structure, confirming that dependency-aware hierarchy (which cascade detection provides) matters more than flat type labels.",
    "issue_2_gm_prm_overlap": "ADDRESSED via precise technical differentiation and head-to-head experiment. Three critical differences from CascadePRM: (1) GM-PRM evaluates each step INDEPENDENTLY -- it checks whether THIS step correctly interprets the image (visual alignment) and whether THIS step's logic is sound (reasoning logic). Cascade errors pass both checks at their own step: the cascade step doesn't misread the image (passes visual alignment) and its reasoning is locally valid (passes reasoning logic). GM-PRM fundamentally cannot detect cascade errors because it never examines cross-step information flow. (2) GM-PRM's dimensions serve as training scaffolding for a generative PRM, producing a single Final Judgment token probability as the score. The dimensions are not structured error labels or classification targets. The paper provides no ablation demonstrating the separate value of visual alignment vs. reasoning logic evaluation. (3) CascadePRM's information flow DAG models dependencies between steps that GM-PRM's step-independent evaluation entirely misses. We add a direct head-to-head experiment: CascadePRM vs. GM-PRM-style dimensional PRM on cascade-heavy problems (geometry, diagram interpretation), specifically measuring cascade detection accuracy where GM-PRM's step-independent evaluation should fail.",
    "issue_3_kappa_fallback": "ADDRESSED via pre-committed granularity ladder with objective cascade criterion. We reduce the core taxonomy from 5-way to 3-way {perception, reasoning, cascade}, targeting kappa > 0.65 (substantial agreement for 3-way). The cascade category is operationalized via the counterfactual criterion ('would this step be correct with corrected perception?'), which is more objective than purely categorical error typing -- it has a testable yes/no answer for math problems.   "title": "Beyond Step-Local Verification: Tracing Perception Error Cascades in Multimodal Process Reward Models",
  "core_problem": "Multimodal process reward models verify each reasoning step independently, missing cascade errors: steps where local reasoning is valid but produces wrong results because upstream visual information was misperceived. When a VLM misreads '45 degrees' as '90 degrees' in step 2, steps 3-7 may apply flawless trigonometry to the wrong angle -- appearing locally correct but systematically producing wrong answers. Cascade errors are invisible to binary correct/incorrect labels, to simple perception/reasoning classification (the cascade step's own reasoning IS correct), and even to Perceval's hallucination detection (no hallucination occurs at the cascade step itself). Across 4+ independent studies, 67-87% of VLM errors originate from visual perception, and each perception error can corrupt multiple downstream steps. Yet no existing verification method detects cascade errors: EVPV explicitly flags step-local cascade tracking as future work; MMErroR explicitly excludes cascading errors from evaluation; PARC models accumulation errors but only in text-only settings. Cascade-aware verification requires a fundamentally new capability: dependency-aware step evaluation that traces visual information flow through reasoning chains.",
  "opportunity": "Three converging developments make cascade-aware multimodal PRMs both timely and feasible. (1) The cascade detection gap is now explicitly acknowledged. EVPV/Grounding the Score (March 2026) uses global reliability signals for visual premise verification but states that 'step-local reliability is an important next step' -- precisely our contribution. MMErroR (Jan 2026) explicitly excludes cascading errors from their benchmark, acknowledging the gap without filling it. Hallucination propagation research (arXiv 2603.27201) empirically shows that cascade errors produce 'locally plausible, internally coherent' steps that mask underlying errors, motivating detection. (2) Text-only cascade detection proves the concept. PARC (Feb 2025) models 'accumulation errors' via premise-augmented DAGs in text-only reasoning, distinguishing root-cause from propagated errors. Conditional Reward Modeling (CRM, 2025) captures causal relationships among reasoning steps. ReasonDiag (March 2026) finds ~44.5% of verification false positives stem from error propagation. These demonstrate that dependency-aware verification is valuable -- extending it to the multimodal perception-reasoning boundary is the natural next step. (3) Dimensional and typed PRM approaches have matured but plateaued at step-independent evaluation. GM-PRM evaluates {visual alignment, reasoning logic} independently per step but cannot trace cross-step dependencies. PathFinder-PRM shows typed labels help in text-only (+2.2 PRMBench) but their ablation reveals that hierarchical structure matters more than category labels alone (-2.8 vs -0.4 on PRMBench). Perceval detects hallucinated spans but treats each step independently. The missing capability across all approaches is dependency-aware verification -- and the multimodal setting, where perception errors cascade from visual processing into reasoning chains, creates the strongest need for it.",
  "landscape": "The landscape segments into five clusters, none occupying CascadePRM's position at the intersection of multimodal perception-awareness and dependency-aware verification.

**Cluster A -- Step-Independent Multimodal PRMs.** Training VL-PRMs (arXiv 2509.23250) provides VL-PRM300K (1.32M steps) with binary labels despite noting 86% perception errors. VisualPRM (arXiv 2503.10291) provides VisualProcessBench (26,950 human labels), binary only. DreamPRM-1.5, TIM-PRM, VRPRM, MM-PRM, URSA all produce binary step scores. All evaluate each step independently without modeling cross-step information flow.

**Cluster B -- Perception-Aware Step-Independent Verification.** Perceval (arXiv 2604.24583, April 2026) detects hallucinated spans via token-level binary classification -- closest existing work, but treats each step independently and cannot distinguish cascade errors from direct errors. GM-PRM (arXiv 2508.04088) evaluates {step intent, visual alignment, reasoning logic} as structured CoT for generative scoring, but evaluations are step-independent with no cross-step dependency modeling; dimensions serve as training scaffolding producing a single Final Judgment score, not structured error labels; and no ablation demonstrates the value of separate dimensions. EVPV/Grounding the Score (arXiv 2603.16253) computes visual reliability via checklist verification, but uses candidate-level (global) rather than step-local reliability, and explicitly identifies step-local cascade tracking as future work.

**Cluster C -- Perception-Aware RL Optimization (Downstream).** PAPO (ICLR 2026, arXiv 2507.06448) uses implicit perception loss via masked-image KL divergence in GRPO -- no PRM involvement. VPPO (ICLR 2026, arXiv 2510.09285) reweights by visual dependency tokens. AT-RL (arXiv 2602.11455), PRCO (arXiv 2603.28618), Perception-R1 (ICLR 2026), PDCR (May 2026), and 'Bad Seeing or Bad Thinking' (ICML 2026 Spotlight) all operate at RL reward/policy level. These consume PRM outputs as scalar rewards; cascade-aware PRM outputs would directly improve the quality of signals these methods consume.

**Cluster D -- Text-Only Dependency-Aware Verification.** PARC (arXiv 2502.02362) introduces 'accumulation errors' via premise-augmented DAGs, distinguishing root-cause from propagated errors -- the closest text-only analog to cascade detection, but no multimodal component. CRM (arXiv 2509.26578) captures causal relationships among text reasoning steps via conditional probability chains. ReasonDiag (arXiv 2603.21286) visualizes error propagation patterns in text-only CoT, finding ~44.5% of verification false positives from error propagation. RewardFlow (arXiv 2603.18859) uses topology-aware propagation in state graphs. All are text-only and do not address the perception-reasoning boundary.

**Cluster E -- Error Taxonomies Without Cascade Detection.** PathFinder-PRM (arXiv 2505.19706) uses {math, consistency} types in text-only PRMs with modest gains (+2.2 PRMBench, but ablation shows category separation contributes only -0.4 vs -2.8 for hierarchical structure). ErrorRadar (ICLR 2025 Workshop) provides {visual perception, calculation, reasoning, knowledge, misinterpretation} for benchmarking MLLM error detection -- never for PRM training. MMErroR (arXiv 2601.03331) defines {visual perception, knowledge, comprehension, reasoning} but explicitly states: 'each sample contains a single, coherent reasoning error... real-world reasoning failures often involve cascading or multiple simultaneous errors.' ThinkWithImages-PRMBench (arXiv 2602.08346) defines 7 error types across 4 categories -- none is a cascade error. All taxonomies evaluate errors at the individual step level without modeling cross-step propagation.

**CascadePRM's unique position**: We bridge Cluster B (multimodal perception-aware verification) with Cluster D (dependency-aware verification) to detect cascade errors -- the gap explicitly acknowledged by EVPV, excluded by MMErroR, and unaddressed by any existing multimodal PRM.",
  "inspired_by": "Three conceptual bridges define CascadePRM's contribution. (1) PARC's accumulation error framework proves that distinguishing root-cause from propagated errors improves text-only verification, but the perception-reasoning boundary in multimodal settings creates a far more impactful instance of this problem: upstream perception failures cascade through downstream reasoning in ways that are mechanistically distinct from text-only logical propagation, because the root cause is cross-modal (visual processing failure) while the cascade is within-modal (text reasoning). (2) EVPV's explicit limitation creates our opportunity: their global reliability signal attenuates all steps uniformly when visual reliability is low, but cascade errors require step-local analysis -- a step that doesn't reference the image at all can still be a cascade error if it uses a value derived from an earlier misperception. The EVPV authors themselves identify step-local reliability as the 'important next step.' (3) PathFinder-PRM's ablation reveals that hierarchical structure (error detection guiding reward prediction) matters more than error type labels alone (-2.8 vs -0.4 on PRMBench). This insight shapes our approach: rather than simply classifying error types, we build a dependency-aware hierarchy where cascade detection (which requires reasoning about cross-step information flow) provides richer structural information than flat type classification. The counterfactual formalization -- 'would this step be correct if the upstream perception were corrected?' -- provides an objective, testable definition of cascade errors that avoids the subjectivity concerns of purely categorical error typing.",
  "approach": "We propose CascadePRM, a framework for detecting and leveraging perception error cascades in multimodal reasoning verification, comprising four interlocking components: (1) a counterfactual cascade detection algorithm, (2) a cascade-annotated benchmark and dataset, (3) cascade-aware PRM training, and (4) downstream integration demonstrating infrastructure value.

**Component 1: Counterfactual Cascade Detection Algorithm (Primary Novelty, Weeks 1-7).**

We formalize cascade errors and build an automated detection pipeline in four stages:

(Stage 1) Visual Claim Extraction: For each step in a solution, extract all claims that reference information derived from the image (e.g., 'angle ABC = 45 deg', 'the bar for 2020 shows 3.2M'). Uses a VLM (Qwen2.5-VL-72B) with targeted prompts to identify visual claims vs. pure reasoning statements.

(Stage 2) Information Flow Graph Construction: Build a directed acyclic graph (DAG) where nodes are reasoning steps and edges connect step j to step k if step k uses a quantity, relationship, or fact derived from visual claims in step j (directly or transitively). This extends PARC's premise-augmented DAG framework from text-only logical dependencies to cross-modal visual-to-reasoning dependencies.

(Stage 3) Perception Error Identification: For each step containing visual claims, verify claims against the image using ensemble VLM voting (Qwen2.5-VL-72B, InternVL2.5-78B, Gemini-2.5-Flash). Steps with incorrect visual claims verified by majority vote are labeled as root-cause perception errors. Dedicated perception verification extracts the specific claim and independently checks it with a focused prompt.

(Stage 4) Counterfactual Cascade Verification: For each downstream step k depending (via the DAG) on a root-cause perception error at step j: (a) extract the misperceived value from step j and determine the correct value; (b) construct a counterfactual prompt: 'Given that [quantity] is actually [correct_value] rather than [misperceived_value], is the reasoning in step k valid?'; (c) if the reasoning IS locally valid (confirmed by 2/3 VLMs), label step k as a CASCADE error; (d) if the reasoning is NOT locally valid, label as a direct error (reasoning, calculation, etc.). This counterfactual test provides an objective, testable definition unprecedented in the multimodal PRM literature.

**Component 2: Cascade-Annotated Benchmark and Dataset (Weeks 2-8).**

(Phase A) Gold-Standard Benchmark -- VisualProcessBench-Cascade: Extend VisualProcessBench's 2,866 samples (~8,000 incorrect steps) with cascade annotations. For each incorrect step, annotators (6 graduate-level, STEM backgrounds) assign: (i) a 3-tier error type {perception, reasoning, cascade} as the core taxonomy; (ii) an optional fine-grained subtype for non-cascade errors {perception subtypes: spatial/numerical/object/attribute; reasoning subtypes: symbolic_formulation/calculation/logical_deduction}; (iii) for cascade errors: the root-cause step ID and the misperceived value. Target inter-annotator agreement: Cohen's kappa > 0.65 for 3-tier classification (substantially above chance for 3-way), with agreement reported at all granularity levels: binary, 2-way {root-cause vs. cascade}, 3-tier, and full fine-grained. The cascade category is operationalized via the counterfactual question ('would this step be correct with corrected perception?'), which is more objective than purely categorical error typing.

(Phase B) Large-Scale Dataset -- VL-PRM-Cascade: Apply the automated cascade detection pipeline (Component 1) to VL-PRM300K (1.32M steps). Confidence-calibrated labeling: HIGH confidence (3/3 VLM agreement, ~70-75%) used directly; MEDIUM (2/3, ~15-20%) used with reduced weight; LOW (~10-15%) routed to human review. Validate against gold benchmark, targeting >80% cascade detection F1.

Pre-committed granularity fallback: If 3-tier kappa falls below 0.60, we report the {root-cause error vs. cascade error} binary taxonomy, which should achieve kappa > 0.70 as a binary classification with an objective counterfactual criterion. This turns a potential weakness into a controlled granularity ablation.

**Component 3: Cascade-Aware PRM Training (Weeks 7-12).**

Train multimodal PRMs (InternVL2.5-8B backbone) with five training regimes forming a granularity ladder:

(A) Binary baseline: standard correct/incorrect on VL-PRM300K.
(B) 2-way typed: {perception error, reasoning error} -- the simplest typed approach, similar in spirit to GM-PRM's dimensional separation but as explicit training labels.
(C) 3-way cascade-aware (PRIMARY MODEL): {perception, reasoning, cascade} with a two-stage prediction architecture inspired by PathFinder-PRM's hierarchical insight: first predict error type (perception/reasoning/cascade), then predict correctness conditioned on error type. For cascade errors, the model additionally predicts the root-cause step, providing interpretable error provenance.
(D) 3-way with cascade-weighted loss: same taxonomy as (C) but with cascade-specific loss weighting. Cascade errors receive higher weight because they represent the largest information gain over binary labels (a cascade step is wrong but for external reasons, requiring different correction strategies). Loss: L = sum_i w(type_i) * CE(y_i, y_hat_i) where w(cascade) > w(perception) > w(reasoning).
(E) Full fine-grained (ablation): complete sub-category decomposition for maximal information, reported for completeness.

Compare against: binary VL-PRM-7B, Perceval (binary hallucination PRM), GM-PRM (dimensional CoT), and EVPV (global reliability gating).

**Component 4: Downstream Integration -- EVPV Enhancement (Weeks 10-13).**

Demonstrate that cascade-aware PRM labels improve downstream verification by enhancing EVPV's framework:

(Integration A) Replace EVPV's global reliability signal with CascadePRM's step-local cascade scores. Instead of attenuating all steps uniformly when visual reliability is low, attenuate only steps identified as cascade-dependent (via the information flow DAG). Steps with no visual dependency path are scored at full weight regardless of global reliability.

(Integration B) Cascade-aware advantage weighting for RL: following DRM's multi-dimensional GRPO framework (arXiv 2510.11457), provide separate advantage signals for perception-error steps (which need better visual grounding) and cascade steps (which need upstream correction, not local improvement). This validates that typed PRM signals can improve RL training -- a mechanism proven feasible by Fine-Grained RLHF (NeurIPS 2023) and POW3R (arXiv 2605.20164) but never demonstrated with multimodal error types.

**Phase 5: Evaluation and Ablations (Weeks 10-15).**

Evaluate on: (a) VisualProcessBench-Cascade: step-level F1 for binary correctness, 3-way error type classification, and cascade detection accuracy (precision/recall/F1 specifically for identifying cascade steps); (b) downstream Best-of-N reranking on MathVista, MathVision, WeMath, ChartQA, PuzzleVQA with N=8,16,64; (c) EVPV integration: step-local vs. global reliability on the same benchmarks; (d) cascade-specific analysis: performance stratified by cascade depth (how many steps from the root perception error), visual modality (geometry/charts/tables), and cascade frequency.

Key ablations forming the granularity ladder: (i) {binary} -> {perception vs. reasoning} -> {perception, reasoning, cascade} -> {full fine-grained} to isolate cascade detection's marginal contribution; (ii) with/without counterfactual verification in cascade detection (does the counterfactual step improve over simple dependency-based cascade labeling?); (iii) cascade-weighted vs. uniform loss; (iv) head-to-head vs. GM-PRM's dimensional CoT approach on cascade-heavy problems; (v) annotation quality: high-confidence-only vs. all labels vs. human-verified.

**Expected Results and Contingency.** Primary hypothesis: the 3-way cascade-aware model (C) will outperform binary PRMs by +3-5 on VisualProcessBench step-level F1 and +2-3 on Best-of-N, with disproportionately large gains on geometry and diagram problems where cascade errors are most frequent. The granularity ladder will show that the {perception, reasoning} -> {perception, reasoning, cascade} step provides the largest marginal improvement, validating cascade detection as the primary value driver. EVPV integration will show +1-2 on benchmarks where EVPV already works. Conservative scenario: if overall gains are modest, the cascade error characterization (frequency, depth distribution, modality stratification) and released artifacts (VisualProcessBench-Cascade, VL-PRM-Cascade, cascade detection pipeline) are publishable contributions as the first empirical study of cascade error propagation in multimodal reasoning verification.",

This phenomenon is invisible to binary labels, simple perception/reasoning classification, and even perception-centric PRMs like Perceval (which detect hallucinations at the error source but not at cascade steps where no hallucination occurs). Based on the search results, here's what I found about Athena-PRM:

## Overview

Athena-PRM is a multimodal process reward model (PRM) designed to evaluate the reward score for each step in solving complex reasoning problems.

## Key Achievement

Athena-PRM sets the state-of-the-art (SOTA) results in VisualProcessBench and outperforms the previous SOTA by 3.9 F1-score, showcasing its robust capability to accurately assess the correctness of the reasoning step.

## Data-Efficient Training

To efficiently generate high-quality process-labeled data, the approach leverages prediction consistency between weak and strong completers as a criterion for identifying reliable process labels. Remarkably, Athena-PRM demonstrates outstanding effectiveness across various scenarios and benchmarks with just 5,000 samples.

## Performance Improvements

The authors also develop two effective strategies to improve the performance of PRMs: ORM initialization and up-sampling for negative data. When using Qwen2.5-VL-7B as the policy model, Athena-PRM enhances performance by 10.2 points on WeMath and 7.1 points on MathVista for test time scaling.

Based on the search results, I found information about the arXiv paper 2605.13467:

PDCR (Perception-Decomposed Confidence Reward) is a framework that aligns the reward structure with vision-language reasoning's heterogeneous nature. It first performs unsupervised skill decomposition, introducing a model-internal Visual Dependence Score to quantify visual reliance.

The Visual Dependence Score is a model-internal signal that quantifies a step's reliance on visual input, and the framework applies an optimal clustering algorithm (Otsu's method) to automatically separate steps into visual perception and textual reasoning groups.

The paper addresses the problem that naively applying a global reward to vision-language reasoning is suboptimal, as the task is a heterogeneous mix of sparse visual perception and dense textual reasoning, creating mixture-induced signal degradation where the training signal for visual steps is statistically distorted by the predominant textual steps.

PDCR computes a decomposed advantage by normalizing confidence gains within each respective skill cluster, ensuring stable, intra-cluster comparison.

**Athena-PRM achieves 65.9 overall F1-score**, significantly outperforming alternatives:
- VisualPRM-8B: 62.0
- Gemini-2.0-Flash: 62.3

input.prompt: Extract ALL key details about PDCR: 1) How does the Visual Dependence Score work exactly? 2) How does unsupervised skill clustering separate perception vs reasoning steps? 3) What are the main results and benchmarks? 4) Does it model cross-step dependencies or cascades? 5) How does it differ from PAPO and VPPO? 6) Any discussion of cascade errors or error propagation? 7) What model is used? 8) Key limitations?

content.content:
# PDCR: Key Details Extraction

## 1) Visual Dependence Score Mechanism
The score quantifies visual reliance by comparing log-probabilities: `V_k^(i) = p_k^(i) - p_{w,k}^(i)`, where the first term represents step likelihood with the real image and the second with a blank (white) image. High scores indicate heavy visual dependence; scores near zero suggest text-driven generation.

## 2) Unsupervised Skill Clustering
The method applies Otsu's algorithm—a classical optimal clustering technique—to the distribution of Visual Dependence Scores. This parameter-free approach "minimizes the total intra-cluster variance" to dynamically find a threshold separating perception (high scores) from reasoning (low scores) steps, achieving 76.2% accuracy against ground-truth labels.

## 3) Main Results & Benchmarks
PDCR achieves 52.9 average accuracy on the 7B model, outperforming PACR (52.2) and GRPO (51.5) baselines. Testing spans seven benchmarks: MMMU-Pro, MMMU, RealWorldQA, VisNumBench, MathVerse, MathVision, and HallusionBench—covering general visual understanding, mathematical reasoning, and hallucination diagnosis.

## 4) Cross-Step Dependencies
The paper does not model cascading dependencies between reasoning steps. It processes each step independently within its skill cluster, normalizing confidence gains only against peers of the same type.

## 5) Comparison to DAPO/VPPO
The paper compares against DAPO (which addresses GRPO's "vanishing advantage" via resampling) but does not discuss VPPO. PDCR outperforms DAPO (52.9 vs. 52.0), suggesting its decomposed reward provides "meaningful, high-quality training signal" beyond stabilization alone.

## 6) Cascade Error Discussion
No explicit discussion of cascade errors or error propagation between perception and reasoning steps appears in the paper.

## 7) Model Used
Experiments use Qwen2.5-VL-3B and Qwen2.5-VL-7B backbones, with additional validation on Qwen3-VL-8B. Training occurs on the Vision-SR1 dataset (~47K examples).

## 8) Key Limitations
The paper acknowledges "mixture-induced signal degradation" from statistical imbalance (30% perception vs. 70% reasoning steps) but offers no discussion of computational scalability, generalization to other vision-language tasks, or robustness when skill distributions differ significantly.

input.prompt: Extract ALL key details about Proof-of-Perception: 1) How is the reasoning DAG constructed? 2) How does conformal prediction work at each node? 3) How does it reduce error compounding? 4) What is the difference from training-time cascade detection? 5) Main results and benchmarks? 6) How does the budget-aware controller work? 7) Any discussion of cascade errors or error propagation in training? 8) Model used? 9) Limitations?

content.content:
# Proof-of-Perception: Key Details Summary

## 1) DAG Construction
The reasoning DAG is generated autoregressively by the MLLM using a small domain-specific language (DSL). "The planner uses the MLLM to autoregressively generate a textual program that encodes the graph" with instructions like CALL_TOOL, FUSE, and RETURN, which a deterministic interpreter parses into an acyclic DAG.

## 2) Conformal Prediction at Each Node
Each node outputs a set-valued prediction rather than a point estimate. A learned nonconformity function s^(t)(x_v, z) scores candidate outputs, and a split-conformal threshold τ_δ^(t) defines sets satisfying "ℙ(z_v^true ∈ Γ_δ^(t)(x_v)) ≥ 1−δ" with marginal coverage guarantees under exchangeability.

## 3) Error Compounding Reduction
PoP maintains multiple calibrated candidates at intermediate steps rather than committing to single predictions. The controller expands computation only when node certificates indicate low confidence, preventing early errors from cascading through the reasoning chain.

## 4) Difference from Training-Time Cascade Detection
Unlike traditional cascades that detect failures post-hoc, PoP proactively uses calibrated uncertainty _during_ inference to guide expansion decisions. Conformal sets are constructed during training via split-conformal calibration on labeled node outputs.

## 5) Main Results
Across DocVQA, TextVQA, InfographicVQA, ChartQA, and MultiDoc2Dial, "PoP improves performance and reliability over strong chain-of-thought, ReAct-style, and program-of-thought baselines" while reducing hallucination by 27–45% relative to the strongest baseline.

## 6) Budget-Aware Controller
The controller π_ϕ observes certificate state (threshold, set size, node type), global budget, and context to choose discrete actions: ACCEPT, RETRY (higher fidelity), EXPAND (additional tool calls), or ABORT. It's trained via policy gradients to balance accuracy and compute cost.

## 7) Error Propagation in Training
PoP uses self-play counterexample mining: "The adversary proposes and executes a reasoning graph, then generates perturbed inputs via controlled visual/layout/tool shifts" and filters for cases where predictions fail or nonconformity is high, enriching calibration with difficult examples.

## 8) Model Used
The planner and fuser are based on a 7–9B open MLLM backbone with tools including PaddleOCR, DETR-like detection, a chart parser, and a layout parser.

## 9) Limitations
"PoP's guarantees are marginal and per-node; answer-level coverage is near-target but not theoretically guaranteed due to composition." Very rare corner cases may require larger candidate sets, and the compute model is simplified (ignoring GPU/CPU overlap and I/O).

Based on the web search results, I found relevant information about error propagation in NLP annotation pipelines:

## Error Propagation in NLP Pipelines

Error propagation analysis in NLP pipelines involves tracing errors through components of pipeline systems, with tasks like entity and event detection, coreference resolution, and semantic-role-labeling being pivotal in high-level semantic tasks.

Since NLP tasks depend on other low-level analysis, the research shows where errors come from and whether they are propagated through different layers.

### Cascading Effects

Poor performance in NLP systems can be primarily a consequence of error propagation. One approach to addressing this problem is Approximate Bayesian Inference for Linguistic Annotation Pipelines, designed to solve cascading errors.

### Joint Inference Solutions

Joint inference over morphology and syntax substantially limits error propagation and leads to high accuracy. This suggests that integrating multiple processing stages rather than keeping them separate can help mitigate multiplicative error effects.

The research demonstrates that understanding error propagation across NLP pipeline stages is crucial for improving overall system performance, and that approaches combining multiple annotation layers can reduce the multiplicative impact of individual component errors.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about DeFacto and its visual grounding methodology:

## Overview

DeFacto is a counterfactual reasoning framework that explicitly aligns visual evidence with final answers. The work addresses the issue that existing methods still fail to ensure evidence-answer consistency, where correct answers must be supported by correct visual evidence.

## Methodology

The approach integrates three complementary training paradigms: positive, counterfactual, and random-masking. The framework develops a language-guided evidence construction pipeline that automatically localizes question-relevant regions and generates counterfactual variants, resulting in DeFacto-100K.

Building on this dataset, MLLMs are trained with GRPO-based reinforcement learning and three complementary rewards to promote correct answering, structured reasoning, and consistent evidence selection.

## Key Dataset and Evaluation

The authors introduce DeFacto-1.5K, a human-annotated benchmark for systematically evaluating evidence-grounded consistency beyond answer accuracy. Experiments on diverse benchmarks demonstrate that DeFacto substantially improves both answer accuracy and evidence-answer consistency over strong baselines.

The research focuses on improving how multimodal language models ground their reasoning in actual visual content rather than relying on spurious text-based patterns.

## Process Reward Models and Annotation Costs

The main challenge in training Process Reward Models (PRMs) lies in obtaining fine-grained step-level annotations, which remain prohibitively expensive. Early work by Lightman et al. pioneered PRM training by employing human experts to label 75K questions at the step level, achieving high-quality results but not scaling automatically due to heavy reliance on manual annotation.

## Cost Reduction Through Active Learning

Recent approaches have made progress in reducing annotation costs. Active and entropy-guided methods demonstrate an order of magnitude reduction in requisite labeling. For example, ACTPRM outperforms prior state-of-the-art models while requiring merely 20% of the annotation costs.

## Cognitive Load in Annotation

Cognitive load is a critical — and often underestimated — challenge. Recent research into interactive and LLM-assisted annotation workflows shows that poorly designed interfaces and unclear annotation logic significantly degrade annotation consistency, especially for non-trivial tasks.

## General Annotation Challenges

Research on AI-assisted human labeling demonstrates that annotation remains inherently time-intensive due to the need for human judgment, verification, and rework at scale. Labeling costs grow non-linearly as task complexity increases, particularly when expert validation is required.

input.prompt: Extract key findings on LLM counterfactual reasoning accuracy: 1) What specific accuracy numbers do different LLMs achieve on counterfactual reasoning tasks? 2) How does counterfactual math reasoning compare to standard math reasoning? 3) What is the accuracy drop from standard to counterfactual? 4) Which models were tested? 5) What types of counterfactual questions were asked? 6) Any findings relevant to whether VLMs can reliably answer "would this step be correct if [value] were changed to [other value]?"

content.content:
# LLM Counterfactual Reasoning Accuracy: Key Findings

## Models Tested
The study evaluated GPT-4o, Qwen-VL, LLaMA-3.2-11B, Gemini-Pro, and DeepSeek-VL across 11 datasets spanning multiple modalities.

## Accuracy Numbers by Task

**Task I (Causal Variable Identification):**
Performance varied dramatically by modality. On text-only datasets, GPT-4o achieved ~89-92% F1 scores, but on code-heavy tasks (Open-Critic), it dropped to 66.2% F1. The paper notes that "LLMs show notable difficulty in identifying the implicit mediator M, which often requires reasoning about the underlying causal pathways."

**Task IV (Outcome Reasoning):**
All models showed "insufficient performance in inferring these implicit variables across all datasets." GPT-4o achieved 85.7% F1 on text-based CRASS but only 62.3% on code tasks (Open-Critic).

## Counterfactual vs. Standard Performance

The research decomposed reasoning into stages rather than comparing direct vs. counterfactual math. However, outcomes under counterfactual conditions (M', Y') consistently underperformed factual reasoning by 5-20 percentage points across datasets.

## Key Finding on VLM Reliability

The authors concluded that "LLMs lack sufficient capacity to reason over causal chains, even when the underlying structure is explicitly provided," suggesting vision-language models struggle with hypothetical value substitution scenarios. Tool-augmented approaches improved explicit variable identification by up to 22.6%, but implicit reasoning remained problematic.

The study evaluated GPT-4o, Qwen-VL, LLaMA-3.2-11B, Gemini-Pro, and DeepSeek-VL across 11 datasets spanning multiple modalities.

**Task I (Causal Variable Identification):**
Performance varied dramatically by modality. On text-only datasets, GPT-4o achieved ~89-92% F1 scores, but on code-heavy tasks (Open-Critic), it dropped to 66.2% F1. The paper notes that "LLMs show notable difficulty in identifying the implicit mediator M, which often requires reasoning about the underlying causal pathways."

**Task IV (Outcome Reasoning):**
All models showed "insufficient performance in inferring these implicit variables across all datasets." GPT-4o achieved 85.7% F1 on text-based CRASS but only 62.3% on code tasks (Open-Critic).

The research decomposed reasoning into stages rather than comparing direct vs. counterfactual math. However, outcomes under counterfactual conditions (M', Y') consistently underperformed factual reasoning by 5-20 percentage points across datasets.

## Controllable and Verifiable Process Data Synthesis for Process Reward Models

The paper proposes a controllable and verifiable framework for synthesizing process supervision data for PRMs (Process Reward Models).

**Core Methodology:**

The framework first constructs a correct symbolic reasoning chain, injects a template-aware error into an intermediate step, recomputes subsequent steps under the corrupted state, and verifies that the injected step is not derivable from its prefix.

**Key Features:**

The resulting paired trajectories are prefix-invalid at the first error while remaining trajectory-consistent after symbolic recomputation, and are translated into aligned natural-language processes for PRM training and evaluation.

**Results:**

Experiments show that the synthesized data improve Best-of-8 reranking on logical reasoning benchmarks and transfer to mathematical reasoning.

The paper was submitted on May 4, 2026, and authored by Yinghui Chi and Lucien Wang from Jilin University.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about SPARE and arXiv paper 2506.15498:

## SPARE Framework

SPARE (Single-Pass Annotation with Reference-Guided Evaluation) is a novel structured framework that enables efficient per-step annotation by jointly aligning solution steps to reference solutions and determining its accuracy with explicit reasoning in single generation.

## Annotation Efficiency

The key innovation of SPARE relates to annotation efficiency. Efficient, high-quality automated process annotation remains a significant challenge, and SPARE addresses this through its single-pass approach. The method achieves competitive performance with MCTS-based methods while offering 2.3× speedup in terms of total token count.

## Applications and Effectiveness

SPARE demonstrates effectiveness across four diverse datasets spanning mathematical reasoning (GSM8K, MATH), multi-hop question answering (MuSiQue-Ans), and spatial reasoning (SpaRP), showing consistent improvements in two applications: (1) training Process Reward Models (PRMs) for ranking and aggregating multiple generations, and (2) fine-tuning models via offline reinforcement learning for greedy decoding.

The paper was authored by Md Imbesat Hassan Rizvi, Xiaodan Zhu, and Iryna Gurevych, with the initial submission on June 18, 2025.

## Current State-of-the-Art

Athena-PRM sets the state-of-the-art (SoTA) results in VisualProcessBench and outperforms the previous SoTA by 3.9 F1-score.

## Beyond Athena: TIM-PRM

Recent advances have gone beyond Athena. TIM-PRM's 8B parameter model significantly outperforms state-of-the-art open-source models (including Qwen2.5-72B and InternVL-78B) and achieves competitive performance with proprietary giants like GPT-4o.

Based on the search results, I found relevant information about "Flying Pigs, FaR and Beyond: Evaluating LLM Reasoning in Counterfactual Worlds," a research paper from 2025.

## Key Findings on Counterfactual Reasoning Accuracy:

**Performance Degradation in Counterfactual Scenarios:**
Evaluation of 11 LLMs across six diverse reasoning datasets reveals a consistent failure: model accuracy plummets by an average of 14% in counterfactual scenarios compared to knowledge-aligned ones.

**The FaR (Flag & Reason) Method:**
The researchers proposed Flag & Reason (FaR), where models are first prompted to flag potential knowledge conflicts before they reason. This metacognitive step is highly effective, narrowing the performance gap to just 7% and increasing overall accuracy by 4%.

**Model-Specific Results:**
The method improves performance across all models with the most noticeable improvement on GPT-4o (G4O) of about 7%.

**Dataset Performance:**
The most dramatic gains are observed on datasets like Hierarchical Syllogisms and KNOT. However, tasks involving deeper chains of reasoning, such as FOLIO, showed less improvement.

The paper demonstrates that while LLMs struggle significantly with counterfactual reasoning tasks due to conflicts between their parametric knowledge and hypothetical premises, the FaR intervention provides a practical and effective solution to improve reasoning in these challenging scenarios.

I've performed a web search on inter-annotator agreement, kappa coefficients, and complex error classification in annotation tasks. Here are the key findings:

## Inter-Annotator Agreement Metrics

For binary and multi-class classification, Cohen's kappa (two annotators) or Fleiss' kappa (three or more annotators) is appropriate. Krippendorff's Alpha (α) is a robust metric capable of handling multiple annotators, various data types (e.g., nominal, ordinal), and missing data.

## Handling Complex Annotation Tasks

For more nuanced situations, weighted agreement coefficients consider the magnitude of disagreement between assigned labels, with Krippendorff's Alpha being frequently used. This is particularly useful since a single value can never capture the complexities of a full annotation task, as different aspects of the annotation will be reliable to varying degrees.

## Multimodal and Complex Settings

The expansion of ML to computer vision, robotics, and multimodal AI has introduced new IAA challenges, with spatial annotations requiring geometric agreement metrics rather than categorical kappa.

## Challenges in Reporting

Many dataset papers report kappa-type coefficients without accounting for class imbalance, sample size, or annotator expertise. Additionally, categorical interpretive conventions do not directly transfer to structured or sequence-labelling tasks, where agreement is inherently lower due to hierarchical or contextual complexity.

The search results don't contain specific information about "time per sample" metrics in annotation studies, but they do emphasize the importance of appropriate metric selection for complex annotation tasks.

I found several relevant research papers from 2026 on VLM (Vision Language Model) capabilities related to visual grounding, premise verification, and question answering:

**Key Findings:**

1. **Visual Premise Verification**: A method called Explicit Visual Premise Verification (EVPV) conditions step scoring on the reliability of visual premises by prompting the policy to produce a step-wise visual checklist, while a constraint extractor independently derives structured visual constraints from the input image.

2. **Grounding Accuracy in VQA**: Research shows a gap between textual accuracy and spatial grounding, with correct answers often lacking reliable localization. VLM models often provide correct answers but rarely correctly indicate where those answers are located.

3. **Visual Attention and Reliability**: Probes on internal states achieve over 92% accuracy at flagging cases where VLM responses are unreliable and can be applied without retraining to identify when a VLM will fail to correctly answer questions requiring multimodal understanding.

4. **Multimodal Reasoning Challenges**: Entanglement between perception and reasoning leads to systematic false positives (rewarding hallucinated visual premises) and false negatives (penalizing correct grounded statements).

These papers suggest that while VLMs show promise in answering visual questions, there remain significant challenges in accurately grounding responses to visual evidence and extracting reliable visual premises.

Based on the search results, here are the key findings regarding error compounding, pipeline accuracy, and the comparison between pipeline versus joint models in NLP information extraction:

## Error Compounding in Pipelines

Errors compound across stages, but existing uncertainty quantification methods either calibrate each stage independently (no joint coverage) or apply a Bonferroni union bound (joint coverage, but conservative). Each stage is trained independently and introduces its own prediction errors that cascade and compound through subsequent stages.

## Pipeline vs. Joint Model Approaches

Joint learning refers to the extraction of entities and classification of relations by a joint model, which can effectively alleviate cascading errors and improve information utilization. However, the joint entity-relationship extraction model based on parameter sharing can effectively reduce the impact of cascading errors on model performance by performing joint learning of entities and relationships in a single model, but it still cannot essentially get rid of the influence of pipeline models and suffers from entity information redundancy and inability to recognize overlapping entities.

Traditional methods deal with this challenge in a pipeline fashion, with each stage model being independently trained. Consequently, the systems lose the capability of sharing information among components, and errors are propagated.

## Information Extraction Applications

Information-extraction (IE) pipelines are among the most widely deployed NLP systems in practice, powering applications in biomedical text mining, financial document analysis, and knowledge-graph population.

**Issue 2 - Pipeline error propagation:**
- The reviewer's concern about 4 stages at 80-85% accuracy each cascading to ~46% end-to-end is mathematically sound, but the stages aren't fully independent
- Errors in the visual claim extraction stage that get missed don't necessarily produce incorrect cascade labels—they just produce missing ones
- I need to conduct a proper error analysis that distinguishes between these different failure modes

, and a pilot study with confidence calibration and partial cascade detection would be essential

**Issue 3 - Missing competitors:**
- PDCR uses a Visual Dependence Score for perception/reasoning decomposition at the RL level, achieving 76.2% on step classification without cross-step dependencies, so it fits in Cluster C
- Proof-of-Perception is more directly comparable—it uses a DAG structure with conformal prediction for inference-time certification to reduce error compounding through set-valued predictions, though its goal differs from mine since it targets inference-time rather than training-time robustness

**Issue 4 - Counterfactual verification reliability:**
- Research shows counterfactual reasoning typically drops 25-40% in accuracy, but my counterfactual task is much narrower—I'm just asking whether a step's arithmetic is correct if a specific value changed, not requiring open-ended reasoning
- This constraint should make the task more reliable than the general case

, and I can simplify it further by providing the corrected computation alongside the counterfactual query
- A pilot study with 50-100 samples would validate this, with symbolic re-execution as a fallback where VLM verification isn't feasible

**Issue 5 - ICLR 2027 deadline:**
- The deadline is September 19 for abstracts and September 24 for full papers in 2026, confirmed through a third-party tracking site and consistent with ICLR's historical pattern

**Issue 6 - Annotation cognitive load:**
- I don't have baseline data on cascade annotation time, so the pilot study needs to measure this
- Cascade tracing is substantially more complex than the binary step labels used in PRM800K, so I'm estimating 3-5 minutes per step versus under a minute for simpler annotations

**Issue 7 - Annotation pilot timeline:**
- I need to build an explicit pilot annotation plan into the proposal

, starting with a 200-step sample in the first two weeks to estimate time, inter-rater agreement, and fatigue effects

Based on the search results, I found the paper you're looking for:

## PASC: Pipeline-Aware Conformal Prediction with Joint Coverage Guarantees for Multi-Stage NLP and LLM Pipelines

PASC (Pipeline-Aware Split Conformal) reduces multi-stage joint coverage to a single scalar conformal prediction problem on the joint maximum nonconformity score.

**The Problem It Addresses:**
Modern NLP and LLM systems are pipelines (such as named entity recognition → entity disambiguation → entity typing, retrieval-augmented generation, and agentic chains), where errors compound across stages, but existing uncertainty quantification methods either calibrate each stage independently (no joint coverage) or apply a Bonferroni union bound (joint coverage, but conservative).

**Key Features:**
- PASC is a pipeline-aware split conformal prediction method that achieves finite-sample distribution-free joint coverage guarantees for multi-stage NLP systems.
- PASC provides a finite-sample distribution-free guarantee that all K stages are simultaneously covered with probability at least 1 - alpha, and is nearly tight up to a 1/(n+1) factor.
- The simplicity of PASC makes it immediately applicable to any multi-stage pipeline: compute per-stage nonconformity scores, take the maximum, and calibrate once.

**Performance:**
On a three-stage NER → NED → entity-typing pipeline over CoNLL-2003, PASC achieves 96.4% end-to-end coverage versus 93.4% for Bonferroni and 86.5% for independent CP, at identical average prediction.

The paper was published recently (about 2 weeks ago) on arXiv as paper 2605.18812.

## Recent Advances in Symbolic Execution and Mathematical Reasoning Verification

Recent work like MATH-VF (from May 2025) leverages external symbolic solvers to verify and refine the correctness of each solution statement.

### Error Detection and Handling

Procedural errors (arithmetic and symbolic manipulation) represent the majority of practical faults in mathematical reasoning, with conceptual errors less frequent but often more damaging (from August 2025 research). Subtle manipulations of reasoning tokens can compromise model outputs, a vulnerability known as "Compromising Thought" (CPT).

### Symbolic Execution Methodology

Symbolic execution executes programs with symbolic inputs instead of concrete values, with execution forking at each branch to check path constraints for satisfiability via SMT solvers.

### Python Symbolic Execution

Symbolic execution faces significant difficulties when applied to dynamically typed languages such as Python, with the major difficulty lying in mapping program execution paths to SMT solver constraints. However, recent approaches combine the generation ability of LLMs with the reasoning ability of symbolic solvers, opening new opportunities in LLM-augmented test case generation.

These results highlight the intersection of symbolic reasoning, automated verification, and cascade error detection in modern mathematical and programming verification systems developed in 2025-2026.

TITLE: "Beyond Step-Local Verification: Tracing Perception Error Cascades in Multimodal Process Reward Models"

CHANGE_TYPE: "major"

CORE_PROBLEM: Same as before but with updated SOTA awareness:
"Multimodal process reward models verify each reasoning step independently, missing cascade errors: steps where local reasoning is valid but produces wrong results because upstream visual information was misperceived. When a VLM misreads '45 degrees' as '90 degrees' in step 2, steps 3-7 may apply flawless trigonometry to the wrong angle -- appearing locally correct but systematically producing wrong answers. Cascade errors are invisible to binary correct/incorrect labels, to simple perception/reasoning classification (the cascade step's own reasoning IS correct), and even to Perceval's hallucination detection (no hallucination occurs at the cascade step itself). Across 4+ independent studies, 67-87% of VLM errors originate from visual perception, and each perception error can corrupt multiple downstream steps. The current VisualProcessBench SOTA (EVPV-PRM at 67.46 F1, Athena-PRM at 65.9 F1) evaluates each step independently -- no existing verification method detects cascade errors. EVPV explicitly flags step-local cascade tracking as future work; MMErroR explicitly excludes cascading errors from evaluation; PARC models accumulation errors but only in text-only settings; Proof-of-Perception uses DAGs with conformal prediction for inference-time certification but not for training-time error labeling. Cascade-aware verification requires a fundamentally new capability: dependency-aware step evaluation that traces visual information flow through reasoning chains."

Just output the JSON with all these fields. Let me provide the rest of the fields:

OPPORTUNITY: "Three converging developments make cascade-aware multimodal PRMs both timely and feasible. (1) The cascade detection gap is now explicitly acknowledged and remains unfilled despite rapid progress. EVPV/Grounding the Score (March 2026) achieves 67.46 F1 on VisualProcessBench using global reliability signals for visual premise verification but states that 'step-local reliability is an important next step' -- precisely our contribution. Athena-PRM (June 2026) achieves 65.9 F1 via data-efficient training with weak-strong completer filtering, but remains step-independent with binary labels. MMErroR (Jan 2026) explicitly excludes cascading errors from their benchmark. Hallucination propagation research (arXiv 2603.27201) empirically shows that cascade errors produce 'locally plausible, internally coherent' steps that mask underlying errors. The SOTA has improved rapidly (62.0 -> 65.9 -> 67.46 F1 on VisualProcessBench) through better data quality and visual grounding, but all improvements are within the step-independent paradigm -- the cascade detection gap persists. (2) Text-only cascade detection proves the concept. PARC (Feb 2025) models 'accumulation errors' via premise-augmented DAGs in text-only reasoning, distinguishing root-cause from propagated errors. CRM (2025) captures causal relationships among reasoning steps. ReasonDiag (March 2026) finds ~44.5% of verification false positives stem from error propagation. These demonstrate that dependency-aware verification is valuable -- extending it to the multimodal perception-reasoning boundary is the natural next step. (3) DAG-based reasoning structures have been validated for multimodal settings. Proof-of-Perception (Feb 2026) models multimodal reasoning as executable DAGs with conformal prediction at each node, reducing error compounding during inference. This validates the structural premise -- reasoning as a DAG with typed nodes -- while targeting a different goal (inference-time certification vs. our training-time cascade labeling). Controllable Process Data Synthesis (May 2026) demonstrates that downstream-propagated errors can be distinguished from source errors in symbolic settings. (4) Perception-aware RL methods have matured but plateau at step-independent decomposition. PDCR (May 2026) uses unsupervised Visual Dependence Scores to separate perception and reasoning rewards via skill clustering, achieving 76.2% step classification accuracy -- but processes each step independently within its skill cluster without modeling cross-step cascades. The missing capability across all approaches is dependency-aware verification -- and the multimodal setting creates the strongest need for it."

**Cluster A -- Step-Independent Multimodal PRMs.** Training VL-PRMs (arXiv 2509.23250) provides VL-PRM300K (1.32M steps) with binary labels despite noting 86% perception errors. VisualPRM (arXiv 2503.10291) provides VisualProcessBench (26,950 human labels), binary only. Athena-PRM (arXiv 2506.09532) achieves 65.9 F1 on VisualProcessBench via data-efficient weak-strong completer filtering with only 5K samples, with ORM initialization and negative up-sampling -- current data-efficiency SOTA but still binary step-independent. DreamPRM-1.5, TIM-PRM (61.7 F1), VRPRM, MM-PRM, URSA all produce binary step scores. All evaluate each step independently without modeling cross-step information flow.

CRM (arXiv 2509.26578) captures causal relationships among text reasoning steps via conditional probability chains. ReasonDiag (arXiv 2603.21286) visualizes error propagation patterns in text-only CoT, finding ~44.5% of verification false positives from error propagation. RewardFlow (arXiv 2603.18859) uses topology-aware propagation in state graphs. All are text-only and do not address the perception-reasoning boundary.

**Cluster E -- Error Taxonomies Without Cascade Detection.** PathFinder-PRM (arXiv 2505.19706) uses {math, consistency} types in text-only PRMs with modest gains (+2.2 PRMBench, but ablation shows category separation contributes only -0.4 vs -2.8 for hierarchical structure). ErrorRadar (ICLR 2025 Workshop) provides multimodal error types for benchmarking, not PRM training. MMErroR (arXiv 2601.03331) defines error types but explicitly states each sample contains a single coherent error, excluding cascading errors. ThinkWithImages-PRMBench (arXiv 2602.08346) defines 7 error types across 4 categories -- none is a cascade error.

**CascadePRM's unique position**: We bridge Cluster B (multimodal perception-aware verification) with Cluster D (dependency-aware verification) to detect cascade errors -- the gap explicitly acknowledged by EVPV, excluded by MMErroR, structurally enabled but not targeted by Proof-of-Perception, and unaddressed by any existing multimodal PRM including the current SOTA (EVPV-PRM at 67.46 F1, Athena-PRM at 65.9 F1)."
